name: Potato Lyrics
tagline: DistroKid's tool for auto-transcribing a song's lyrics and time-syncing them for streaming platforms.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Appears bundled with a DistroKid distribution membership rather than sold standalone.

verdictSummary: The technical core here is a solved problem: a local Whisper model with word-level timestamps will transcribe a vocal stem and spit out a synced LRC or TTML file in an afternoon. Accuracy on clean vocals is genuinely decent, and you can stem-separate first to make it better. What you cannot build is the part that matters commercially: getting those synced lyrics accepted and displayed on Spotify, Apple Music and friends, which runs through distributor and lyric-aggregator pipelines you have no seat at. So if you want a lyric file for a video, a karaoke screen or your own archive, build it. If you want the words scrolling under your track on Spotify, you are paying a distributor either way.
coreLoopDIY: Feed it an audio file, get back a word-timestamped transcript exported as plain text, LRC and TTML, with a tiny local editor for fixing the lines Whisper invented.
requirements: A machine that can run faster-whisper (GPU helpful, CPU fine for a few songs)
Patience for manual correction of mumbled or layered vocals
whatYouLose: Delivery: your file does not reach Spotify or Apple Music lyrics without a distributor in the loop
Platform-specific formatting rules and rejection feedback, which are undocumented and change
Automatic association with your release metadata and ISRC
Human-grade accuracy on dense mixes, ad-libs and stacked harmonies
One button in a dashboard you already log into anyway
moatNotes: The transcription is commodity. The pipe from a transcription to a lyrics panel on a streaming service is not, and it is gated by distribution agreements.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because artists are not buying a transcript, they are buying placement. Synced lyrics on streaming services flow through aggregators and distributors, and if you already pay for distribution, the lyrics tool is a free checkbox inside a workflow you cannot bypass. A local Whisper script gives you a perfect file and no destination for it.
notes: Rare case where the hard part is free and the easy part is locked behind a business relationship.
prompt:
Build a local command line tool called lyricsync that transcribes a song and produces time-synced lyric files.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, dependencies managed with uv
- faster-whisper for transcription with word_timestamps enabled
- demucs (htdemucs two-stem mode) for optional vocal isolation
- ffmpeg via subprocess for audio decoding and resampling to 16kHz mono wav
- click for the CLI, no framework beyond that

Commands:
- lyricsync transcribe PATH --model large-v3 --isolate-vocals --lang en
  Decodes the input, optionally runs demucs and keeps only the vocal stem, transcribes with word timestamps, writes a JSON file next to the input holding segments and per-word start and end times.
- lyricsync export PATH --format lrc|ttml|txt
  Reads the JSON and writes the chosen format. LRC uses line-level [mm:ss.xx] tags. TTML uses word-level timing spans wrapped in a minimal tt document. txt is plain lines, no timings.
- lyricsync edit PATH
  Serves a single static page on localhost:7788 that plays the original audio, highlights the current line, lets the user fix text and nudge line start times, and saves back to the JSON. Plain HTML, vanilla JS, one file, no build step, no npm.

In scope: local files only, batch of one song at a time, sane defaults, a --help that actually explains the formats.
Out of scope: accounts, cloud anything, telemetry, uploading to any streaming service or lyric aggregator. Do not pretend a distributor pipeline exists.

Be explicit in the README that Whisper hallucinates on instrumental passages and stacked vocals, and that the edit step is mandatory, not optional.
No secrets are needed; if you add any config, read it from .env.
Ship a README with install steps, one worked example, and a note that models download on first run.
